title: Arrays
description: Store ordered collections of values, access items with zero-based indexing, append with push(), and transform data cleanly with map() and filter().

objectives.statement: Access elements using zero-based bracket indexing and append elements using push().
Transform every element of an array into a new array of corresponding values using map().
Filter array elements based on a boolean predicate into a new subset array using filter().

content.title: Ordered Sequences of Data
content.hook: Managing individual variables like lesson1, lesson2, lesson3 quickly breaks down at scale.
content.context: Arrays allow you to hold an ordered list of items in a single structure. Each item has a position called an index. You can append new items, transform every item with map(), or pick matching items with filter().
goals: Understand zero-based index positioning in JavaScript arrays.
Append elements using push() in-place mutation.
Transform array items with map() and select elements with filter().

content.title: Array Mechanics: Mutation vs Transformation
content.description: Visual diagram comparing push(item) which mutates the existing array in-place, map(fn) which returns a brand new transformed array of equal length, and filter(predicate) which returns a brand new subset array containing only items passing the condition.

feedback.correct: Spot on! filter selects [2, 8] and map doubles them to [4, 16].
feedback.incorrect: filter first keeps only even numbers [2, 8], and map doubles each to [4, 16].

hints.content: filter keeps only numbers where n % 2 === 0 (even numbers), resulting in [2, 8].
map multiplies each surviving even number by 2, yielding [4, 16].

content.question: What happens to the original array `scores` when you run `const highScores = scores.filter(s => s >= 70);`?

options.text: The original `scores` array remains completely unchanged; `filter` returns a newly allocated array.
The original `scores` array is permanently reduced to only contain items >= 70.
JavaScript deletes `scores` from memory and replaces it with `highScores`.
The items under 70 in `scores` are converted to `null`.

items.text: Evaluate users identifier to retrieve the original array
Execute filter callback on each user and construct intermediate array of active users
Execute map callback on each active user in the intermediate array to extract names
Assign the resulting new array of string names to the const names variable

In getPassingScores, return scores.filter(s => s >= threshold);

content.title: Build Array Processing Helpers
content.prompt:
Implement three utility functions:
1. addCourse(courses, newCourse): Appends newCourse to the courses array using push and returns the updated array.
2. formatBadges(topics): Uses map() to transform an array of strings (e.g. ['html', 'css']) into upper-case tags (e.g. ['[HTML]', '[CSS]']).
3. getPassingScores(scores, threshold): Uses filter() to return only numbers greater than or equal to threshold.

feedback.correct: Well analyzed! Declarative methods like map and filter make data transformations explicit and avoid off-by-one errors.
feedback.incorrect: Please provide at least 30 characters discussing readability and when loops might still be useful.

content.prompt: When is it preferable to use map() and filter() over a manual for loop, and when might a traditional loop still be necessary?

content.title: Arrays Takeaway
takeaways: Arrays represent ordered sequences with 0-based indices from 0 to array.length - 1.
push() appends items to an array in place, while map() and filter() return new arrays without mutating the source.
map() transforms every element 1-to-1; filter() selects elements based on a boolean predicate.
